title: Short Stuff: Corduroy
summary: Short Stuff episode on corduroy. The hosts discuss the disputed origin of the name (French "cord du roi" versus the Brooks Brothers claim of eighteenth-century English streetwear), and the older fustian fabric tied to al-Fustat in Egypt. They cover the first US corduroy production in Woolsaston, Massachusetts around 1780, the Corduroy the Bear children's book, and how corduroy is made: a third pile yarn is woven in, then cut into ridges (wales). They explain whale count, pink cord, and the fabric's history of fashion, class associations, car upholstery, and revivals. The episode ends with a reading recommendation.

entities.name: Read Between the Lines of the Wailed Fabric

segments.title: Opening banter and corduroy origin debate
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter, then introduce corduroy and debate its name origin. They weigh the French 'cord du roi' idea against the Brooks Brothers claim of eighteenth-century English streetwear, and mention the older fustian fabric linked to al-Fustat, Egypt.

segments.title: Corduroy history and Corduroy the Bear
segments.summary: The hosts describe early thick pile fabrics and the first US corduroy production in Woolsthorpe, Massachusetts around 1780. They discuss the Corduroy the Bear children's book and personal stories about homemade clothes.

segments.title: Whale count and corduroy types
segments.summary: The hosts explain whales as the raised ridges and that a higher whale count means finer ridges. They discuss fine-whale Oxford shirts and pink cord, and talk about how corduroy wears at the knees.

segments.title: How corduroy is made
segments.summary: The hosts explain the weaving process: a third set of pile yarn is woven into a base fabric, then cut into rows, which exposes the base fabric in valleys between raised ridges. They call it a three-dimensional pile weave, comparable to velvet and terry cloth.

segments.title: Corduroy fashion history and revivals
segments.summary: The hosts discuss corduroy's popularity in the fifties, sixties, seventies, nineties, and two-thousands revivals, its class associations shifting from upper-class sportswear to working-class wear, and its use in car upholstery starting in the twenties. They also share personal clothing anecdotes.

segments.title: Sign-off and reading recommendation
segments.summary: The hosts recommend the book Corduroy: Read Between the Lines of the Wailed Fabric by James Smith, available from Headles, and sign off.
